title: The Sharpe Pint: Slack Water, Trapped Cash, and the Microstructure of Trend

opening_mood.text: Happy Saturday, and welcome to your morning briefing. While our friends across the pond spent Friday nursing early Independence Day hangovers, the rest of the world kept spinning—and the data didn't stop dropping. We have got a cooling US jobs market, a quiet surrender in the Strait of Hormuz, and a private credit market that is starting to look a bit like a crowded pub exit at closing time.

Grab a coffee (or a pint, we won't judge on a Saturday) as we dive into how these moves shape your Monday morning meetings, why your LBO models might be lying to you, and the microstructural reason why short-term trend following has been such a dog.

content.text: While the US took Friday off, the global macro machine kept grinding. From a cooling US jobs market to a quiet surrender in the Strait of Hormuz, here are the key stories you need to know to sound like the smartest person in the room on Monday.
1. US June Jobs Report: Slower hiring, shrinking labour force

The US labour market is officially cooling down. June nonfarm payrolls added a meager 57,000 jobs, roughly half of the 110,000 consensus forecast. To make matters worse, the Bureau of Labor Statistics shaved a combined 74,000 off April and May's figures in downward revisions. The headline unemployment rate did tick down to 4.2% (from 4.3%), but don't let that fool you—it fell because 720,000 people packed up and left the labour force entirely, dragging the participation rate down to 61.5%.

Why it matters: This is a classic 'soft landing' signal that threads the needle for the Federal Reserve. It is weak enough to ease concerns about demand-driven inflation, but not quite disastrous enough to scream recession. Average hourly earnings rose 0.3% month-on-month (3.5% year-on-year), which is stable but still lagging behind recent inflation prints.

The City angle: Fixed income and macro desks loved this. Short-dated Treasuries rallied as the soft print took the immediate pressure off the Fed to hike rates. With new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at the helm, the market is betting the central bank will keep its finger off the trigger for now, though a rate hike before year-end isn't entirely off the table.

What to say: 'The drop in unemployment to 4.2% is a bit of a mirage—it was entirely driven by 720,000 people dropping out of the labour force. But with payrolls coming in at just 57k and revisions shaving off another 74k, the Fed under Kevin Warsh has some breathing room. It takes the pressure off immediate rate hikes.'
2. The Strait of Hormuz: Free passage is dead, and the bill is coming

The 60-day toll-free grace period negotiated in the June 17 framework (following the US-Iran war earlier this year) is ticking away, and Tehran has made its next move. Iran's parliament is drafting legislation to impose a permanent $2 million transit fee per vessel passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Oman is desperately trying to negotiate a workaround, proposing voluntary 'service fees' for navigation and safety to keep things legal under Article 43 of the Law of the Sea. But Iran is holding firm on mandatory tolls, potentially payable in Chinese yuan or Bitcoin to bypass US sanctions. Bloomberg reports that major European powers are quietly accepting that their ships will have to pay, while the US and Gulf states are screaming blue murder.

Why it matters: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's ultimate energy bottleneck, carrying roughly 20% of global oil and LNG. Ending centuries of free transit and slapping a $2 million-per-voyage tax on shipping will structurally raise global energy and logistics costs. If Europe rolls over and pays, it sets a highly dangerous precedent for other critical waterways like the Malacca Strait.

The City angle: This is a structural inflation story. Energy and commodity desks are watching the August 16 expiration date like hawks. Shipping equities and marine insurers are already repricing risk, and any permanent fee regime will act as a structural tax on global trade, keeping energy prices elevated even as broader demand cools.

What to say: 'The 60-day grace period on the Strait of Hormuz expires in mid-August, and Iran has made it clear: free passage is history. While Oman is trying to dress it up as voluntary service fees to keep the lawyers happy, Tehran wants a mandatory $2 million toll per ship, potentially in yuan or Bitcoin. If Europe is already quietly rolling over to pay, we're looking at a permanent structural tax on global energy.'
3. Trump Allies Renew Push to Reshape the Fed

On June 29, the US Supreme Court handed down a pair of massive rulings on presidential power. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Court overruled a 91-year-old precedent (Humphrey’s Executor), giving the President at-will authority to fire the heads of independent agencies like the FTC. However, in Trump v. Cook, the Court carved out the Federal Reserve, ruling 5-4 that President Trump could not unilaterally fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook without 'cause' and proper notice. Undeterred, Bloomberg reported on July 3 that Trump’s allies are already treating the ruling as a procedural roadmap, redoubling their efforts to push Cook out and targeting former Chair Jerome Powell to clear the way for more loyalists.

Why it matters: Central bank independence is the bedrock of global financial markets. If the executive branch successfully weaponises 'cause' to purge the Fed Board, monetary policy becomes highly politicised. That threatens the credibility of the US dollar and could inject a massive political risk premium into Treasury markets.

The City angle: For macro strategists and bond traders, this is the ultimate tail risk. A politicised Fed that cuts rates on presidential command would destroy the inflation-fighting credibility of the central bank. While Kevin Warsh is now Chair, a Board packed with political appointees would make his job incredibly difficult and rattle international investors.

What to say: 'The Supreme Court's Trump v. Cook ruling was a 5-4 win for Fed independence, but Trump’s allies are already treating it as a how-to guide rather than a stop sign. They're looking to use the court's procedural roadmap to push out Lisa Cook and target Jerome Powell. If they succeed in politicising the Board, Kevin Warsh's job as the new Chair gets a lot more complicated, and bond markets will start pricing in a massive political risk premium.'
4. UK Credit Card Defaults Hit Highest Level Since 2009

The Bank of England’s Q2 Credit Conditions Survey, released on July 2, revealed a worrying spike in consumer distress. High street lenders reported that defaults on credit cards and other unsecured loans rose sharply, with a net balance of 37.4% of lenders reporting rising delinquency rates, up from 18.6% in Q1. This is the highest level of credit card defaults since the global financial crisis in 2009. Interestingly, defaults on secured loans (like mortgages) remained completely flat.

Why it matters: This paints a stark picture of a 'K-shaped' squeeze on British households. Homeowners are doing whatever it takes to keep a roof over their heads—cutting back on everything else to pay the mortgage. Meanwhile, lower-income households are increasingly relying on plastic to cover daily essentials, and they are officially hitting a wall. High interest rates, persistent inflation, and a cooling job market are finally taking their toll.

The City angle: This is a red flag for retail banking, consumer credit, and asset-backed securities (ABS). Lenders are already tightening credit availability for Q3 to mitigate risk. For equity analysts, it suggests that UK consumer discretionary spending is set for a rough ride, even if mortgage rates start to ease slightly.

What to say: 'The Bank of England's latest credit survey is a sobering read. Credit card defaults have surged to their highest level since the 2009 financial crisis, with a net 37% of lenders reporting a rise in delinquencies. It's a classic K-shaped squeeze: mortgage defaults are flat because people will do anything to keep their roof, but the reliance on plastic to cover daily costs has officially hit a wall. If you're looking at consumer ABS or retail banking credit risk, the red lights are flashing.'
5. Private Credit's Liquidity Squeeze: $14 Billion Trapped

The $1.8 trillion private credit market is facing a serious reality check. In Q2 2026, a wave of redemption requests has left more than $14.5 billion of investor capital trapped across over a dozen funds, while direct lenders only paid out $8.6 billion. That means funds are locking up roughly $1.70 for every $1 an investor successfully reclaims. The squeeze stems from pent-up demand after giants like Blue Owl Capital imposed 5% withdrawal caps last quarter, alongside growing investor anxiety over asset quality—particularly exposure to the AI-disrupted software sector.

Why it matters: Private credit has been the darling of the yield-starved asset management world, promising high returns with 'low volatility'. But that low volatility was always a function of not marking assets to market. Now, the 'liquidity illusion' of retail-oriented private credit vehicles (like BDCs) is breaking. Funds are being forced to restructure (Blue Owl is moving to a 'return of capital' model) and execute massive loan asset sales to raise cash.

The City angle: This is a classic liquidity mismatch. Investors who treated private credit as a liquid alternative are learning the hard way that you can't easily exit a direct loan portfolio. For asset managers, this redemption backlog will suppress new capital inflows and force a rotation back into liquid public markets or tangible assets like real estate and infrastructure.

What to say: 'The private credit redemption wave is getting serious. In Q2, over $14.5 billion of investor capital got trapped in funds, while only $8.6 billion was paid out—that's $1.70 locked up for every dollar returned. Retail-focused vehicles like BDCs promised liquidity they simply can't deliver when everyone runs for the exit at once. If you're in wealth management or private debt, the liquidity illusion of these vehicles is officially dead.'
6. Blackstone's QTS Abandons "World's Largest" Data Center

In a major setback for US AI infrastructure, Blackstone-backed QTS Realty Trust has officially terminated its planned Digital Gateway data center project in Prince William County, Virginia. The project was envisioned as the world's largest data center campus, spanning 2,100 acres and up to 37 buildings. However, after years of intense local opposition, environmental lawsuits, and a court ruling invalidating its zoning approvals, QTS threw in the towel. Compass Datacenters (backed by Brookfield) had already pulled out in May, leaving QTS to face massive utility upgrade costs alone.

Why it matters: This is a stark reminder that the bottleneck for AI isn't just Nvidia's chip supply—it's the physical reality of power, water, local zoning, and legal battles. It also comes amid growing market anxiety that tech giants are overbuilding data centers before seeing clear commercial returns on their massive AI capital expenditure.

The City angle: For infrastructure and real estate private equity, the era of easy 'greenfield' data center development is over. Future build-outs will have to focus on brownfield sites or regions with pre-secured power and less local resistance. It also highlights the value of existing, fully leased hyperscale assets—which explains why Digital Realty just agreed to buy back Blackstone's stakes in three other Virginia data centers for $3.5 billion.

What to say: 'Blackstone's QTS pulling the plug on the Virginia Digital Gateway is a massive reality check for the AI buildout. This was supposed to be the world's largest data center campus, but years of local lawsuits and zoning defeats finally killed it. It shows that the real bottleneck for AI isn't just Nvidia's supply chain—it's the physical reality of power, water, and local NIMBYs. You can't run LLMs in the cloud if you can't get the concrete poured.'
7. Trump Blocks USMCA Renewal, Triggering a 10-Year Countdown

On July 1, the mandatory six-year joint review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) took place. While Mexico and Canada supported extending the free trade pact for another 16 years, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. 'did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form.' This triggers an annual review process, starting a 10-year countdown. The agreement remains fully in force until July 1, 2036, but the refusal to extend it introduces significant policy uncertainty. The U.S. is pushing for stricter Rules of Origin (ROO) requirements—particularly in the automotive sector (wanting to raise regional content from 75% to 82%, with 50% specifically from the U.S.)—and measures to block Chinese goods from exploiting the tariff-free zone.

Why it matters: The USMCA governs nearly $2 trillion in North American trade annually. While day-to-day trade operations won't change immediately, the lack of long-term certainty will delay major corporate investment decisions. It also signals a highly protectionist stance that could disrupt integrated supply chains, especially in automotive, manufacturing, and agriculture.

The City angle: This is a major headache for automotive and industrial equity analysts. Highly integrated North American supply chains are built on the assumption of frictionless trade. The shift to annual reviews means companies will have to model year-by-year tariff risks, which will likely suppress capital expenditure and hit the Mexican Peso and Canadian Dollar.

What to say: 'Trump's refusal to extend the USMCA isn't an immediate death blow—the deal is still fully in force until 2036—but it officially starts a 10-year countdown of annual reviews. The U.S. is using this to squeeze Canada and Mexico for tougher terms, especially on auto parts and blocking Chinese backdoor imports. For corporates with highly integrated North American supply chains, the era of long-term trade stability is over, and we're back to year-to-year policy anxiety.'

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: It was a short but spicy week on Wall Street, wrapping up with a quiet Friday as US markets shut their doors for the Independence Day long weekend. But before traders headed off for their beers and barbecues, Thursday served up a double-whammy of market-moving drama: a shockingly weak US jobs report and a fascinating divergence between the old-school Dow and the high-flying tech giants.
The 'Slack Water' Jobs Report

The big macroeconomic event of the week was Thursday's June Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP) report, which came in colder than a British summer. The US economy added just 57,000 jobs in June, a massive miss against the consensus forecast of around 110,000. To make matters worse, the previous two months of hiring were revised down by a combined 74,000 jobs (April down to 148,000 and May down to 129,000). On paper, the headline unemployment rate actually ticked down slightly to 4.2% from 4.3% in May. But don't let that fool you: this wasn't driven by a hiring boom, but rather by a massive 720,000 people dropping out of the labour force entirely, dragging the participation rate down to 61.5%. It is what economists call 'slack water'—the tide isn't coming in or going out; it is just standing still.
The Cross-Asset Playbook: Bad News is Good News (Unless You’re a Chipmaker)

The market's reaction to the jobs miss was a classic textbook display of 'bad news is good news' for interest rates, but with a twist. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1.1% to close at a fresh record high of 52,900.07, as the soft data took the pressure off borrowing costs and boosted rate-sensitive, old-economy stocks. However, the S&P 500 finished virtually flat at 7,483.24, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.8%. Why the split? We saw a heavy dose of profit-taking in the semiconductor and artificial intelligence winners that have carried the market all year, leading to a healthy rotation into broader sectors.

Across other asset classes, the cross-asset read was highly consistent. Short-dated US Treasuries rallied hard (meaning yields fell) as traders dialled back expectations of further rate hikes. The US Dollar sold off in response to the weaker yields. In commodities, gold caught a bid on the back of lower rate expectations, while Brent crude hovered around $72 a barrel. Oil has collapsed from its March peak of $120, largely driven by progress in technical peace talks between the US and Iran in Doha, which has significantly defanged global energy-driven inflation.
Warsh in Sintra: Independence Day Comes Early

All of this macro softening gives the newly minted Federal Reserve Chair, Kevin Warsh (who took the reins on May 22, 2026), some much-needed breathing room. Speaking at the ECB's annual Forum on Central Banking in Sintra, Portugal, earlier in the week, Warsh made a point of asserting the Fed's fierce political independence. He essentially told President Trump 'no dice' on immediate, politically motivated rate cuts, vowing that the Fed is committed to its 2% inflation target. However, Warsh did concede that inflation risks and expectations 'have come down' in recent weeks. With June's weak jobs print in hand, Warsh now has the perfect cover to keep rates on hold without looking like he is bowing to political pressure.
The Global Ripple: Friday's Quiet Churn

With US cash markets closed on Friday, July 3, the rest of the world was left to digest the US data. European shares were mixed, with Germany's DAX rising 0.4% to 25,667.73, while London's FTSE 100 slipped 0.4% to 10,613.55. The real action was in Asia, where tech stocks staged a dramatic relief rally after a brutal couple of sessions. South Korea's Kospi—which had plunged nearly 8% on Thursday—snapped back like a rubber band, jumping 5.8% on Friday. Heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix surged 8.2% and 10.9% respectively, proving that when the market leans too heavily to one side, the snapback can be violent. Tokyo's Nikkei 225 also advanced 1.5% to close at 69,744.07.
What This Means for the Pub Chat

items: The Fed's Pause Button is Locked: Warsh wants to look tough, but a +57k jobs print means further rate hikes are effectively off the table. Expect a 'high-for-longer' plateau rather than a steep tightening cycle.

The Great Rotation is Real: The Dow hitting records while the Nasdaq falls is the textbook definition of profit-taking in mega-cap tech flowing into the rest of the market. It is a healthier, broader market, even if your tech-heavy portfolio took a minor ding.

Unemployment is a Mirage: The drop in the headline unemployment rate to 4.2% is a statistical quirk driven by people leaving the workforce, not finding jobs. The labour market is cooling faster than the headline suggests.

sections.title: Financial Idea of the Day: The Interest Tax Shield Cap

content.text: The Interest Tax Shield Cap: Why EBIT vs. EBITDA Matters for LBOs

If you have ever built a Leveraged Buyout (LBO) model, you know the holy grail of leverage is the interest tax shield. Because interest expense is tax-deductible, the government effectively subsidises your debt. The formula is simple: your tax bill is reduced by your interest expense multiplied by the tax rate. But tax authorities are not stupid. They do not want private equity firms buying companies, loading them with debt, and paying zero corporate tax. To stop this, regulators globally capped how much interest you can actually deduct.
The Battle of the Acronyms: EBIT vs. EBITDA

Under Section 163(j) in the US and the Corporate Interest Restriction (CIR) in the UK, interest deductibility is generally capped at 30% of the company's earnings. But the devil is in how you define those earnings. Historically, the US cap was 30% of EBITDA. But in 2022, the US rules tightened the definition to 30% of EBIT (excluding depreciation and amortisation). This was a massive blow for capital-intensive businesses (think manufacturing, infrastructure, or telecom) because they have huge depreciation charges. By forcing them to use EBIT, their allowable earnings base shrank, meaning they could deduct far less interest. However, in a major turn of events, the US permanently restored the friendlier EBITDA-based calculation starting in 2025 via the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). Meanwhile, the UK has stuck to its CIR rules, capping deductions at 30% of tax-EBITDA, subject to a £2 million de minimis.
A Simple Mathematical Walkthrough

Let us look at how this actually hits the numbers. Imagine a capital-intensive UK portfolio company with EBITDA of £100m, Depreciation & Amortisation (D&A) of £40m, and EBIT of £60m. The private equity sponsor funds the acquisition with £500m of debt at an 8% interest rate, resulting in £40m of annual interest expense. The corporate tax rate is 25%.

items: Under the EBITDA-based cap (30% of EBITDA): The maximum interest you can deduct is £30m (30% of £100m). Out of your £40m interest expense, £30m is deductible and £10m is disallowed (though you can carry it forward). Your tax shield is £7.5m (£30m multiplied by 25%).

Under the EBIT-based cap (30% of EBIT): The maximum interest you can deduct drops to £18m (30% of £60m). Now, £22m of your interest is disallowed. Your tax shield shrinks to just £4.5m (£18m multiplied by 25%).
The Damage: The shift from EBITDA to EBIT costs the company £3m in extra cash taxes in a single year. That is £3m less cash available to pay down debt, dragging down your equity IRR.

content.text: Why This Matters in the City

If you are interviewing for private equity or investment banking roles, this is a classic differentiator question. Anyone can explain a basic LBO, but explaining how interest deductibility caps alter the optimal capital structure shows you actually understand real-world deal-making. If a target company's interest expense exceeds the 30% cap, the after-tax cost of debt rises because you lose the tax shield on the excess. This makes heavy leverage less attractive and forces sponsors to write larger equity checks, directly lowering returns.
Common Beginner Mistake

The most common mistake in financial modeling is assuming all interest is automatically tax-deductible. Beginners will simply calculate tax as EBIT minus interest expense, multiplied by the tax rate. If you do this without building an interest deductibility schedule, you will overstate your free cash flow, overstate your debt paydown capacity, and present a model that would get laughed out of an investment committee.
Over a Pint: How to Sound Smart

If you are modeling a UK mid-market deal, you have got to watch the CIR rules. While the £2 million de minimis protects smaller deals, any serious leverage on a capital-intensive business is going to hit that 30% tax-EBITDA cap fast. If you are not modeling the disallowed interest carryforwards, your IRR is basically a work of fiction.

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA)

content.text: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA)

Picture this: you’ve spent months training a state-of-the-art deep learning model to forecast EUR/USD or SPY. It’s a beauty. You push it to production, and then—bam!—the Bank of England hikes rates unexpectedly, or inflation numbers come in hot. Suddenly, your frozen model is behaving like a tourist trying to navigate Bank station at 8:45 AM on a Tuesday: completely lost and making terrible decisions.

In quantitative finance, we call this the non-stationarity problem. Markets shift regimes, and models trained on yesterday's calm waters sink in today's storms. The traditional fix is to retrain the model periodically. But that's slow, expensive, and by the time the retraining is done, the market has probably shifted again. Enter Test-Time Adaptation (TTA).

The core idea of TTA is simple: instead of freezing your model completely during deployment, you let it adapt its parameters on the fly using the incoming, unlabeled stream of live market data. But you don't retrain the whole thing—that would be a recipe for 'catastrophic forgetting' (where the model forgets everything it learned during training) and would melt your servers. Instead, you freeze the heavy 'backbone' of the neural network and only update a tiny fraction of the parameters—specifically, the normalization layers (like Batch Norm or Layer Norm scale and shift parameters).

A recent paper by Wu et al. (2026), 'Test-Time Adaptation for Non-stationary Time Series: From Synthetic Regime Shifts to Financial Markets', digs into exactly how to make this work for financial data. For direction classification (e.g., 'is the index going up or down today?'), they adapt the model by minimising the entropy of its predictions on recent windows, forcing it to make confident bets. For regression (e.g., forecasting volatility), they use consistency regularization—minimising prediction variance across slight variations of the input. To stop the model from going completely rogue, they add a quadratic drift penalty (which acts like a leash, keeping the adapted parameters close to the pre-trained ones) and an uncertainty-triggered fallback to reset the model if things go pear-shaped.
Mini Technical Example: Adapting Norm Layers in PyTorch

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# 1. Load your pre-trained model
model = load_pretrained_forecaster()

# 2. Freeze the backbone, only train the normalization layers
model.eval() # Set to eval mode
for module in model.modules():
    if isinstance(module, (nn.BatchNorm1d, nn.LayerNorm)):
        module.train() # Keep norm layers in training mode to adapt
        module.weight.requires_grad = True
        module.bias.requires_grad = True
    else:
        module.requires_grad_(False) # Freeze everything else

# 3. Define a lightweight optimizer for test-time updates
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(filter(lambda p: p.requires_grad, model.parameters()), lr=1e-3)

# 4. Test-Time Adaptation Loop (Causal)
def adapt_and_predict(x_test_window):
    # x_test_window is the recent unlabeled market data (e.g., past 5 days)
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    
    # Forward pass
    predictions = model(x_test_window)
    
    # Loss: Minimize entropy (for classification) to force confident predictions
    probs = torch.softmax(predictions, dim=-1)
    entropy_loss = -torch.sum(probs * torch.log(probs + 1e-6), dim=-1).mean()
    
    entropy_loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    
    # Now make the actual forecast for the next step
    with torch.no_grad():
        next_forecast = model(x_test_window[-1:])
    return next_forecast
The Interview / Watercooler Angle

If you're interviewing for a quant research or machine learning role at a fund, a classic question is: 'How do you handle regime shifts or non-stationarity in production?' Most candidates will give the standard, boring answer: 'I'd set up a pipeline to retrain the model every weekend.' If you want to stand out, you say: 'Periodic retraining is a lagging indicator. I'd look at Test-Time Adaptation (TTA). By freezing the backbone and only optimizing the affine parameters of the normalization layers on the fly—using an entropy-minimization loss or consistency regularization—we can adapt to shifting market regimes in real-time with virtually zero computational overhead. To prevent parameter drift, I'd implement a quadratic penalty relative to the source weights and an uncertainty-triggered fallback.' That is an instant pass. It shows you understand both the theoretical machine learning concepts and the practical, low-latency constraints of production finance.
Risks & Caveats

TTA isn't a free lunch. The biggest risk is over-adaptation or parameter drift. Financial markets are notoriously noisy. If there is a temporary flash crash or a brief liquidity squeeze, an aggressive TTA model might over-adapt to this noise, thinking we've entered a permanent new regime. When the market mean-reverts a few hours later, the adapted model will get absolutely slaughtered. In fact, Wu et al. (2026) noted that in real financial markets (like SPY and EUR/USD), aggressive adaptation can sometimes hurt performance. Often, simply updating the running batch-normalization statistics (the mean and variance) without updating the weights themselves is the most robust default.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: If you work in or around the City's quant scene—perhaps dodging the rain outside a pub in EC2 while debating whether AHL or Winton has the better Sharpe ratio—you'll know that short-term trend following has been a bit of a dog since the financial crisis. The standard excuses are wheeled out like tired cliches: 'too much money in the trade,' 'central banks ruined volatility with QE,' or 'the robots took over.' But a brand-new paper from the heavyweights at Capital Fund Management (CFM) and Imperial College London completely upends these narratives. It turns out the death of short-term trend is actually a story of market plumbing—specifically, how high-frequency traders (HFTs) interact with different order books.
The Paper

The paper is titled 'Is Trend Still Your Friend?: A Microstructural Account of the Demise of Short-Term Trend-Following' (published on arXiv on 2 July 2026), co-authored by Jutta G. Kurth, Zoltan Eisler, Adam Rej, and the godfather of econophysics himself, Jean-Philippe Bouchaud.
The Core Discovery

The authors analyzed roughly 100 liquid futures contracts from 1995 to 2025. They confirmed that post-2008, short-term trend PnL collapsed. However, they discovered a fascinating dichotomy: the collapse only happened on 'small-tick' contracts (where the tick size is tiny relative to daily volatility, creating a sparse order book with many price levels). On 'large-tick' contracts (where the tick size is large relative to volatility, creating a dense order book with massive queues at a few price levels), short-term trend-following remained highly profitable and intact. Neither asset class nor simple liquidity explains this split.
The Self-Fulfilling Loop

To explain why this matters, the authors model trend following as a self-fulfilling prophecy. When trend followers get a buy signal, they buy. This aggressive buying pressure has a market impact, pushing the price up further, which in turn reinforces the trend signal. The profitability and persistence of the trend are actually sustained by this very price-impact channel.

Trend signals trigger directional trades, whose market impact reinforces the very price moves that generated the signal. Both the profitability and the persistence of trend are therefore both sustained by the same impact channel.

But this loop requires trend followers to be able to execute aggressively at a reasonable cost. Post-2008, market making transitioned to HFTs. In small-tick (sparse) books, when HFTs detect predictable directional flow (like trend followers executing), they rapidly fade their quotes (withdraw liquidity), causing massive slippage. This made aggressive execution too expensive, forcing trend followers to pull back. Once they pulled back, the self-fulfilling loop broke on the input side: the price-impact reinforcement disappeared, and the trend signal itself decayed. In large-tick (dense) books, the massive queues at each price level prevent HFTs from easily fading, so the loop continues to operate.
Key Takeaways

items: The death of short-term CTAs is not a macro story about central banks or simple capacity constraints. It is a microstructural story.
The critical variable for trend survival is the volatility-normalised tick size.
Market anomalies are not passive mispricings; they are active feedback loops. Your own trades can create the trend, and if you stop trading, the trend disappears.
Systematic models cannot treat all assets the same based on asset class or simple liquidity. You must group them by tick-size dynamics.

content.text: What to Skim vs. What to Read

Skim the heavy mathematical derivations of the price-impact models and the exact formulas for book imbalance correlations in the middle. Focus your reading on Section 4 (the empirical split between small-tick and large-tick contracts) and Section 6 (the explanation of the HFT feedback loop).
How to Use It

If you are interviewing for a quant or macro role, this is absolute gold. When asked about CTA performance or market efficiency, you can say: 'Everyone blames QE or capacity for the death of short-term CTAs, but Bouchaud's recent paper shows it is actually a microstructural issue. In small-tick books, HFTs fade their quotes when they see trend flow, which broke the self-fulfilling price-impact loop. In large-tick books, the queue depth protects the loop, so trend still works.' It shows you are reading the absolute latest research and understand the plumbing of the markets, not just the headlines.
Our Take

This is a mind-bending way to think about market efficiency. It proves that market anomalies are dynamic ecosystems. The idea that trend-following actually creates the trend through its own market impact—and that changing market-maker behavior can kill the anomaly by breaking the feedback loop—is brilliant. It's a masterclass in why microstructural details trump macro narratives.

sections.title: The Omission Bias: Why Doing Nothing is the Ultimate Corporate Shield

content.text: The Concept: Passive Disasters vs. Active Mistakes

Ever wondered why your firm is still using a legacy database that looks like it runs on MS-DOS, or why a portfolio manager will ride a dying stock all the way to zero while refusing to swap it for a better prospect? Welcome to the Omission Bias. Famously mapped out by psychologists Jonathan Baron and Ilana Ritov, this bias is our hardwired tendency to judge harmful actions (commission) far more harshly than equally harmful inactions (omission).

In plain English: if you actively do something and it blows up, you get crucified. If you do absolutely nothing and things slowly rot away, people barely notice—or at least, they don't blame you nearly as much. It is the ultimate psychological shield for the risk-averse corporate survivor.
The Finance Example: The 'Safe' Bleed
Consider two portfolio managers, PM A and PM B, both managing £100m funds:

items: PM A holds a legacy retail stock. Over two years, the stock slowly bleeds 40% of its value due to structural decline. PM A does nothing. Clients grumble, but they chalk it up to 'macro headwinds' and 'sector rotation'. PM A keeps their job.

PM B inherits the same stock, immediately spots the structural decline, sells it, and reinvests the cash into a promising mid-cap. Two weeks later, a surprise regulatory change hits the mid-cap, and it drops 40%. PM B is hauled over the coals by the investment committee for 'reckless trading' and 'poor stock selection'.

content.text: The financial damage to both funds is identical. But because PM B took an active step (commission), they bear the psychological and professional blame. PM A’s passive disaster (omission) is excused as bad luck. This asymmetry explains why so many professionals prefer a slow, comfortable decline over a calculated risk.
How to Use It at Work
You can use this understanding to manage upwards, pitch better, and stand out in interviews:

items: When pitching a change: If you are trying to get your MD to approve a new system, a new hire, or a portfolio rebalance, don't just pitch the upside of the action. You must actively frame 'doing nothing' as a risky, active decision. Calculate the 'Cost of Inaction' (COI) and put a hard pound figure on it. Force them to realise that maintaining the status quo is a trade they are actively putting on every single day.

In interviews: When asked how you manage risk or make decisions under pressure, explain how you combat omission bias. Tell the interviewer: 'I treat holding a position with the exact same analytical rigour as buying it. If I wouldn't buy it today at the current price, I shouldn't be holding it.' It shows a level of institutional maturity that most junior candidates lack.

content.text: One Line to Remember
Doing nothing is still a trade—it’s just one you didn't have to fill out a ticket for.
